title: Failure
hook: Peter, Paul, David, Moses all failed badly

segments.voice: Yesterday, loneliness: God setteth the solitary in families, and from the cross, behold thy mother. Your line was set in families. Who did you call, text or knock for? Day one thousand four hundred one.

A short list of résumés. One man killed someone and fled the country. One took another man's wife, then arranged for the husband to die in battle. One went house to house dragging believers off to prison. One promised he would never deny his friend, and then did, before the cock crowed. Moses. David. Paul. Peter. These moments are written down in scripture, in plain sight, for anyone to read. And none of their stories stops there. Today: failure.

Begin with Peter, because his story has a strange order to it. Before the denial even happens, Jesus tells him in Luke: "I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren." The comeback is spoken before the fall. Then Peter denies him, the cock crows, and "Peter went out, and wept bitterly." Later, by the sea in John's Gospel, the risen Jesus asks him, "Lovest thou me?" and gives him a job: "Feed my sheep." Next, David. The prophet Nathan tells him a story about a rich man who steals a poor man's only lamb. David is furious. Then Nathan says it: "Thou art the man." David answers, "I have sinned against the LORD." The heading of Psalm 51 ties that psalm to this moment, and it holds the line: "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." The story is honest that consequences stay. But it keeps going. Then Moses. He killed a man and ran to Midian. And it was there, keeping someone else's sheep, that the bush burned and the call came. The call found a man who had run. Last, Paul. He never pretends the past didn't happen: "I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God." And then the very next sentence: "But by the grace of God I am what I am." Failure is not final doesn't mean failure didn't matter. Peter wept. David's house suffered. But in each story, the failure is a chapter, and the book goes on.
screen: `THE CALL FOUND A MAN WHO RAN.`
`BY THE GRACE OF GOD I AM WHAT I AM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive yourself one failure. Settle, and breathe. Choose one failure you keep replaying. Not necessarily the biggest; one that still stings. Look at it honestly, the way Paul named his: this happened, and it was mine. If it hurt someone and you can still make it right, set that aside as a job for later. Then, for now, put down the punishment. If you pray, you can say David's line: create in me a clean heart, O God. If you don't, tell yourself plainly: that was a chapter, not the end. The bell holds the time.
Failure. Falling short, sometimes badly. In scripture Moses, David, Paul and Peter all fail, and every one of their stories keeps going.
Your line: failure is not final. Today, when that old failure replays, answer it the way Paul did: name it honestly, then say the next sentence. Day one thousand four hundred one.

howItsDone: Christians bring their failures to God in confession, privately or in a service, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians also confess to a priest and receive absolution; Psalm 51 is used as a prayer of repentance in several liturgies.

myth: the Bible hides its heroes' failures
David's sin, Peter's denial and Paul's persecution of the church are all written down plainly.
Paul calls himself the least of the apostles
because I persecuted the church of God. but by the grace of God I am what I am.
Moses was called at the burning bush before he ever failed
he had killed a man and fled; the call came while he kept sheep in Midian.

fork.setup: you're Peter. you denied Jesus three times. now the risen Jesus is on the shore asking, lovest thou me? what does he do next?
options: give you a job: feed my sheep.
fork.reveal: he asks, and each time gives Peter work: feed my lambs, feed my sheep. the one who failed is sent to care for others.

original.note: Hebrew: I have sinned — David's answer to Nathan in 2 Samuel 12:13.

trapdoor: what you thought: real people of faith don't fail badly.
what it means: Moses, David, Paul and Peter all failed in plain sight, and scripture keeps telling their stories past the failure.
what a scholar hears: in Luke, Jesus says 'when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren' before the denial. the comeback is spoken before the fall.

notes: 'Denied Jesus three times' (fork) rests on Luke 22:34 and 22:61 ('thrice'); John 21:17 says 'the third time'. Confirm.
Psalm 51's heading links it to Nathan's visit after Bathsheba; the lesson says 'the heading ties that psalm to this moment' rather than asserting David's authorship as historical fact. Confirm.
Moses 'killed a man and ran to Midian' (Exodus 2:11–15): the text says he killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew; the lesson keeps it brief. Keeper may want the context added.
'David's house suffered' summarizes 2 Samuel 12:10–14 and what follows; confirm.
howItsDone: 'in many liturgies' — soften if needed.
Audit: Peter 'promised', not 'swore', never to deny Jesus (Matthew 26:35, Luke 22:33); his swearing comes in the denial itself (Matthew 26:74).
Editor pass: cut "their worst moments" (superlative); fork reveal now matches John 21:15–17 (lambs, then sheep); varied the practice opener; removed the "two minutes" time claim from the practice.
